The International Energy Agency (IEA) warns that global datacentre carbon emissions are on track to rise by 70% within four years, driven largely by the US and China turning to fossil fuels to power their artificial intelligence expansion. The Paris-based agency projects that datacentres will consume twice as much electricity by 2030 compared with today, with AI accounting for three-quarters of this growth. Within those four years, AI datacentres alone are expected to add an extra 350 terrawatt-hours of annual electricity consumption, exceeding the yearly usage of Great Britain. The report also notes that global energy prospects have grown less certain following what it describes as the greatest energy market disruption in history stemming from a Middle East war.

IEA executive director Fatih Birol stated there is no credible pathway for the energy system to return to its previous state, arguing instead that policy decisions made after the crisis will reshape demand driven by population growth, air-conditioning needs, and a booming AI economy. Although datacentre developers have become the world's largest corporate buyers of renewable energy through grid connections, fossil fuel appetite is expected to grow even faster in some regions. By 2030, roughly half of China's AI datacentre electricity will come from coal plants, with renewables supplying the remainder alongside smaller contributions from nuclear and gas.

In contrast, the US is projected to rely on gas for about 60% of its datacentre power by 2030. In August this year, plans were announced for approximately 180GW of new gas-fired plants linked to US datacentres, nearly matching total installed EU gas capacity at that time. Fossil-fuel generation growth is driving the projected emissions increase, and US developers' appetite for gas power exceeds that of Canada by more than 16 times, where plans call for just 11GW of gas generation. Elsewhere globally, AI developers have proposed new gas plants totaling only 4GW combined capacity.

Renewables are expected to play a larger role outside the US and China: in the EU, datacentres should rely on renewables for about 70% of electricity by 2030, followed by nuclear power, gas generation, and minimal coal. The IEA based its forecasts on AI server shipment data that has climbed eighteen-fold since 2020, along with space-based imagery tracking the construction of 93 large "AI factories" worldwide.

The agency's analysis indicates global datacentre capacity rose tenfold over the past two years to 17GW. Once completed, these AI factories are expected to hold about 50GW combined capacity. The existing stock now totals 120GW, with 80% located in China, the US, and the EU. Under what is considered the IEA's central base case scenario, a further 120GW will be built by decade's end, three-quarters of which would be AI datacentres.
items.title: IEA Warns Datacentre Carbon Emissions to Rise 70% by 2030

South Korea became the fourth country to surpass annual exports of US$1 trillion, joining Germany (2006), the United States and China (2007), after cumulative figures crossed the threshold at 2.09pm on Nov 19. The milestone came a year after first topping US$700 billion in 2025 and marks the first new entrant to the trillion-dollar club in 19 years, driven by surging semiconductor prices and shipments amid global artificial intelligence spending. President Lee Jae Myung hailed the achievement as the culmination of generations of effort, paying tribute to workers who spent their youth in garment factories, shoe plants and shipyards, while pledging that growth benefits large and small companies across the country and calling for sustained competitiveness in key industries alongside AI and biotechnology.

The Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources projects full-year exports at US$1.17 trillion, up about 65% from a record US$709.3 billion in 2025. Exports totalled US$930.2 billion over the first 10 months, including US$396.8 billion in semiconductors that accounted for roughly 43% of the total and nearly tripled the previous record for the period. AI data centre demand drove up DRAM and NAND prices while lifting shipments of solid-state drives, transformers, cables and copper.

Exports excluding chips rose 20%, with 16 of 20 major categories gaining; cosmetics exports reached US$12.4 billion in 10 months, topping the 2025 full-year record. Shipments rose in seven of nine major markets, led by China up 88% and the United States up 77%, while small and midsize companies also posted record exports. Imports rose 21% to US$635.1 billion, leaving a surplus of about US$295 billion through October against US$77.4 billion for all of 2025.

Deputy minister Kang Kam-chan noted that much of the record reflects higher prices rather than greater output, as AI demand sent memory chip prices soaring and petroleum product export prices jumped 62% to US$1,105 a ton. He acknowledged profits have gone mostly to large companies due to structural limits in chips and petrochemicals, which have short supply chains and employ relatively few workers unlike automobiles or ships, regretting that gains had not flowed through to suppliers.

Kang said exports could exceed US$1 trillion again in 2027, though easing chip and oil prices could pull them below the 2026 level. He expects AI infrastructure demand to hold through the third quarter of 2027, with delays in US data centre projects, Chinese competition and protectionism remaining risks.

Kang described a structural shift as Korea's major industries matured from selling ships, frozen fish, plywood and clothing when exports first passed US$10 billion in 1977 toward AI-driven markets for power equipment, copper and aluminium alongside chips. He argued the export structure must gradually shift toward overseas investment to build strategic ties with trade-deficit-sensitive partners such as the United States under Donald Trump's administration, while keeping research and "mother factories" at home rather than simply following Japan's path after the 1985 Plaza Accord.
items.title: South Korea's Exports Surpass US$1 Trillion for First Time

Google DeepMind released Gemini 4 Neon, a reasoning model positioned between Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen in the Gemini 4 family. It targets coding agents, knowledge work, and science workflows with a developer pitch of near-frontier scores at lower cost per task. The pricing is $3 per 1M input tokens and $15 per 1M output tokens.

Neon features a 1M-token unified context with a 64K default output limit, expandable to up to 1M via background long decode. It runs on Google-hosted infrastructure only; weights are closed, so there are no local GPU, quantized, or edge builds available. Inputs cover text, images, audio, and video, with a knowledge cutoff of March 2026.

The model exposes multiple thinking levels: High is the default, while xhigh is reserved for the hardest engineering, analytical, and science workloads. For long agent runs, Neon supports context compaction and reduces redundant file reads. In Google Antigravity, it can act as an orchestrator directing parallel Gemini 4 Hydrogen subagents on smaller tasks.

Google reports all benchmark scores without independent reproduction. On the AA Intelligence Index, Neon scored 61, ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 at 59 and GPT-6.2 Sol at 57. It reached #1 on the AA Coding Agent Index at 58.6, with SWE-sweep using a provider harness hitting 39.0% versus 10.1% for Opus 5.5. In knowledge work it scored 56.3% on Zapier AutomationBench against 42.5% for Opus 5.5, and 75.8% on Agents' Last Exam v1.1.

In science and reasoning, Neon achieved 84.0% on RiemannBench, 70.5% on Terminal-Bench-Science, and 71.3% on HLE-Diamond. Its strongest result was 95.2% on GraphWalks for long-context recall (covering 256K to 1M context), versus 80.1% for GPT-6.2 Sol and 66.8% for Opus 5.5.

Neon does not win every benchmark. Claude Opus 5.5 leads Terminal-bench 4.1 at 65.8% against Neon's 65.2%, and FrontierCode 2.0 at 47.3% versus Neon's 46.2%. GPT-6.2 Sol leads Chartography at 75.1% versus 73.5% for Neon.

On the Vals Index, Neon scored 70.9% and ranked #2; on the Agent Arena index it also ranked #2 with a score of 1336.

Google states that Neon at high thinking costs 32% less per task than Carbon, and claims 50% to 80% lower cost per task versus rivals on Vals Index and Agent Arena. At xhigh, Google cites 36%+ lower cost than rivals at their highest settings. These are described as per-task claims rather than per-token prices.

For comparison, GPT-6.2 Sol lists at $2/$10 input/output; Claude Opus 5.5 lists at $4/$20; and Gemini 4 Carbon is priced at $2/$10 until November 30, then $4/$20 per 1M tokens.

Developers can access Neon through the Gemini API paid tier via Google AI Studio and Android Studio, Gemini for business via API and model dropdown, Google Antigravity for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers, and the Gemini app for Pro and Ultra subscribers.

On safety, Google reports a 0.09% misaligned action rate on its agentic safety suite, passing 99.2% of the agent honesty evaluation, with a 0.0% attack success rate on Gray Swan's prompt injection benchmark at the highest thinking level. Its shortcut rate of 2.45% on a coding cheating test is described as the lowest among any Gemini 4 model.

The article notes that all scores are self-reported by Google and not independently reproduced, with AA scores for Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.2 Sol matching Artificial Analysis.
items.title: Google DeepMind Releases Gemini 4 Neon

items.summary: David Chiem, founder of Singapore-listed MindChamps Preschool, has launched an investment platform called MindFunds that is seeking A$100 million (S$86.2 million) for its first fund dedicated to acquiring and developing purpose-built pre-school properties in Australia. The company has sold 45 franchise licences as part of its Australian expansion, and the new fund will acquire or develop sites where franchisees can open and operate their centres. MindChamps operates pre-schools, after-school care centres, and therapy services for children, and it is present across Asia including Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Myanmar. Goh Seh Harn, chief executive officer of Trigger Asset Management, which advises on the fund, said the company targets a first close in the first half of 2027 and plans a follow-on fund of A$500 million.
items.title: MindChamps launches MindFunds to raise capital for Australian preschool expansion

items.summary: On 18th November 2026, Google introduced Gemini 4 Neon to its existing Gemini 4 lineup of Hydrogen, Argon, and Carbon. The author noted that the series' pricing had already been confusing, with Argon and Carbon previously priced identically while Hydrogen cost three-quarters of that price but was set to fall to one-quarter once the other two models doubled their prices on 1st December after initial discounts expired. Neon complicated this further by omitting Argon from its promotional materials; Google's new lineup image listed only Carbon, Neon, and Hydrogen from most to least expensive. In reality, because Carbon was then at half price while Neon cost $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, Neon was the priciest of the three, ahead of Carbon ($2/$10) and Hydrogen ($1.50/$7.50), with these figures changing once Carbon doubled to $4/$20 on 1st December. The author tested all three reasoning tiers of Neon at low, medium, and high levels using pelican images as the test set, finding that Neon outperformed Hydrogen but fell short of Carbon. Separately, running an extra effort level in Google Antigravity against Gemini 4 Neon produced a Three.js animation depicting Yonkers rising as a mech to stomp across Manhattan, Queens, and Brooklyn while using OpenStreetMap data.
items.title: Google's Gemini 4 Neon pricing and benchmarking

items.summary: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella argued at The New York Times DealBook Summit that the rise of AI agents will reshape the economics of the internet and disrupt business models built around advertising. He compared this shift to the earlier transition from web portals like Yahoo to search engines like Google, saying it would change which companies pay others for traffic and transactions. According to Nadella, aggregators whose model was designed for what he called the “human web” will be reshuffled, and monetization based on eyeballs may give way to cost-per-click or transactional wins. He added that if a company does not accept AI agents, competitors who do will capture the advantage. The discussion then turned to Amazon’s decision to block AI agents from accessing its retail website, preventing them from browsing its catalog and making purchases for users. Nadella suggested that companies protecting their existing models could lose ground to those more willing to embrace agents, using Shopify as an example of a platform that might allow agents while gaining an advantage if Amazon keeps blocking them. He characterized the situation as competitive scrambling over business models across categories.
items.title: Nadella on AI agents reshaping web economics

items.summary: Anthropic priced its long-awaited initial public offering at $83 per share, above its stated range of $70 to $78, which the article frames as a sign of strong investor appetite despite market jitters following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure. The company sold 980 million shares in the offering, up from the 825 million initially planned, generating $81.3 billion in proceeds and surpassing SpaceX's $75 billion record to become the largest IPO in history by proceeds raised. At the IPO price, Anthropic is valued at roughly $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis, an increase from the $965 billion reached in May during its last private round that raised $65 billion, but below the $2 trillion reportedly targeted several months earlier. The company will begin trading Thursday on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT." A strong first day would signal continued investor optimism about AI adoption despite recent volatility in AI-driven stocks. The article notes Anthropic's performance may set expectations for its rival OpenAI, which was last valued at $1.25 billion and has not announced IPO plans. Although no venture capital investor holds more than a 5% stake, the offering is a windfall for backers including Sequoia, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC, Iconiq, Menlo Ventures, Coatue, Sound Ventures (launched by Guy Oseary and Ashton Kutcher), and Spark Capital. Some existing investors—Sequoia, Iconiq, Lightspeed, Accel, and Altimeter Capital Management—are reportedly planning to buy billions of dollars' worth of shares in the IPO. Strategic partners Amazon and Google hold nearly 15% and almost 14% respectively, while a group including AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC Partners agreed to purchase $26 billion worth of non-voting shares through a private placement alongside the offering. The seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei, each sold nearly 3.4 million shares in the IPO for about $282 million each.
items.title: Anthropic prices record-setting IPO at $83 per share

The A-Team Group, whose awards are voted on by capital markets practitioners, named Databricks winner of Best AI Solution for Data Intelligence & Governance at the 2nd annual AI in Capital Markets Awards 2026. It was Databricks' first award from this program. Angela Wilbraham, CEO of A-Team Group, said: "Congratulations to Databricks for winning Best AI Solution for Data Intelligence & Governance..." The recognition centers on combining AI with governance on a single platform rather than offering raw intelligence or automation.

The article frames the industry as drawing a line between experimental AI and production-grade AI that can withstand regulatory scrutiny. It cites elevated intraday volatility, T+1 settlement in North America compressing operational windows, ESMA's supervisory briefing on algorithmic trading, and the FSB's 2026 work program on AI sound practices as pressure points. A 2026 survey of managers overseeing roughly $2 trillion in assets found that 94% already use AI or machine learning in their alternative data research process, while 71% cite combining data from different sources as their most frustrating challenge.

The piece argues the competitive edge lies not in large language models but in proprietary data. It presents RBC Capital Markets' Aiden QuickTakes agent on Databricks, which unifies data ingestion, AI-driven analysis, and content generation to auto-generate draft research reports up to 95% faster; Michael Tran of RBC said: "Every firm in capital markets has access to large language models. The difference is whether you can point them at your own proprietary data with the right controls in place." LSEG partnered with Databricks so AI agents can query 350,000+ investments using plain English and turn hours of manual fund screening into minutes.

Other use cases include unified cybersecurity analytics platforms centralizing structured, semi-structured, and unstructured security data for threat detection, forensics, and compliance reporting; core banking migrations to a governed lakehouse with OpenSharing and Unity Catalog replacing spreadsheets and manual reconciliations. Databricks Genie One is presented as the front end letting portfolio managers, analysts, and risk officers ask questions in plain language with answers grounded in Unity Catalog without SQL or notebooks. Through the Model Context Protocol, the same layer extends to Microsoft Teams, Excel, and assistants such as Claude and ChatGPT, with every request authorized against Unity Catalog permissions and logged.

The article concludes that firms can adopt new models without disruption because their proprietary data foundation is already governed; it offers a FAQ covering who won, what the platform includes, why governance matters, and how MCP applies to financial services. The piece reads as vendor-promoted content rather than independent reporting.
items.title: Databricks Wins A-Team Award for AI in Capital Markets

Google DeepMind shipped Gemini 4 Neon, its fourth Gemini 4 model in roughly seven weeks, joining the retired Argon and the dead Pro and Flash models from earlier generations. The naming is based on atomic weights: Carbon (6) is the flagship tier while Neon (10) is a midtier that costs less to run than Carbon despite technically outperforming it by some measures due to distillation, RL, and benchmarking effects. Pricing for Neon is $3 per million input tokens, $0.15 for cached input, and $15 for output, with a 1M-token context window and four effort levels; Vals reports a maximum output limit of 1M tokens. Rollout covers the paid Gemini API in AI Studio and Android Studio, Gemini for business, Antigravity for Pro and Ultra subscribers, and within the Gemini app it is selectable as 'Deeper analysis,' including for Tasks. Day-one integrations include Cursor, GitHub Copilot across its app, CLI and VS Code, and LangChain Managed Deep Agents. Arena recorded gaps of 28 days between Argon and Carbon, 15 between Carbon and Hydrogen, and six between Hydrogen and Neon.

On independent benchmarks, at high effort Neon matched Carbon's Intelligence Index score of 60 for $3.74 per task; on GDP.pdf it scored 33.4% at high versus 28.0% at xhigh. In Agent Arena Neon debuted second with 1,336 points across about 4,200 sessions and a $2.82 median task cost, placing second on steerability while Carbon still leads the separate Text Arena. On Vals it placed second on the Vals Index at 70.9%, roughly 0.4 points behind Fable 5.2 at less than half the cost per task; on Code Migration Neon averaged 160 turns versus Carbon's 234 and Hydrogen's 574, scoring below both. On CursorBench 4.1 it scored 63.7% at default effort, up from Hydrogen's 57.3%. In 13 early Antigravity sessions Kimmonismus recorded 762 tool calls with a 93% input-cache hit rate; when told to avoid the terminal Neon ran zero shell commands, though logs also showed 57 capacity errors and four stalled runs.

In hands-on use Theo reported using Neon for copy while Fable implements changes and Astra plays tests, and Jeremy Howard praised Neon while reverting Solveit's Astra and Sol options to their pre-6.2 versions; Reddit readers debated whether Neon becomes the everyday replacement for Gemini 3.1 Pro now that Google has separate tiers for fast work versus harder projects.

Separately, new results were reported for GPT-6.2 models: on MathArena Astra took first and Sol second, with Astra solving 42 of 53 ArXivLean problems; Vals reports what it believes is the first formalization in Lean of Smoktunowicz's Gap Theorem, checked by an independent kernel replay. In Agent Arena Astra debuted sixth while Sol placed eleventh at a $0.90 median task cost; on Code Arena WebDev Astra placed third at 42% lower median cost than its predecessor. OpenAI opened a public beta for GPT-6.2 Responses API jobs with two-hour and eight-hour targets carrying 30% and 40% discounts per token, respectively. Tibo Sottiaux said early reviewers used builds from before the final days of changes; Artificial Analysis found Astra's responses got shorter and it was less likely to admit uncertainty in behavioral evaluation.

In open weights and inference, a correction to Pi adapter numbers raised solves on the 51 hardest SWE-bench Pro tasks from 15-32 to 20-33 (39.2% to 64.7%) after Hugging Face reran affected tasks following a tunnel outage that hit nine base-model runs; an OpenCode adapter moved Qwen3.8-27B from 35.3% to 51.0% on the same subset with thinking off. Tencent released Hy4 Flash weights, a 224B-parameter multimodal MoE activating 12B parameters per token, supporting 1M context and including roughly 64B n-gram embedding table, in instruct, FP8 and base checkpoints. vLLM 0.34.0 enables extensible KV cache by default with Model Runner V2 as the sole GPU runner, reporting up to 1.95x faster NVFP4 decoding on GB200. Epoch estimates chip capacity for a fixed basket of agent workloads grew 4.6x from Q2 2025 to Q2 2026 versus 2.6x peak 8-bit compute; Runway cut serving hardware in half, reporting a 57B video model at 24 fps on four GPUs down from eight; Prime Intellect launched Model Factory for RL, supervised fine-tuning, serving and evals; Hugging Face released the message dataset from its 1,000-agent PyBot project.

In research and chip design, OpenAI reports up to 14% improvement against optimized baselines on blocks of AMD's flagship GPU design using Synopsys tools for verification, with some changes entering a manufacturing-bound design; OpenAI also published an update on internal agent use and proposed regular disclosure of AI research acceleration indicators. A DAIR study found that in a 40-issue held-out test a gated approach editing one module at a time scored 40.0% on SWE-bench Lite at 46.7K tokens per task versus 42.5% for a full rewrite at 451.6K; MAC Bench found most gains from eight agents came from parallel exploration, with Opus 5.5 the sole tested model to show added gain from coordination.

In media and voice, Genie 4 reached Project Genie as Google's world model adds native audio and lets users change the world with text mid-session for eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers; Inworld released weights for a voice-isolation model and its SAVA turn detector detecting completed turns in median 71 ms at 48 kHz (64M-parameter offline, 58M real-time); AssemblyAI split its 3.7 release into models for voice agents, live transcription and recordings; Kling Image 4.0 placed seventh in Artificial Analysis's text-to-image rankings and sixth in editing.

In industry, Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share above the initial range covering 980M shares worth about $81.3B, with roughly $79.4B from pre-fees shares sold by Anthropic; Nasdaq trading under ANT is expected November 19. Palo Alto Networks agreed to buy Applied Compute in a $4.5B all-stock deal for post-training and serving open-weight models, expecting to close in its fiscal Q3 2027 subject to regulatory clearance.

In the Reddit recap on local audio, Blue TTS v3 is an MIT-licensed model generating audio at about 50x real time on CPU; AudioGhost lets users describe a sound in text and separate it from a recording via Meta's SAM-Audio. On local inference and coding, TokenWing claims to stream most routed experts from SSD with one user reporting 45-50 tok/s on a 120B MoE using 12 GB VRAM and 32 GB RAM; pairing GPT-6.2 Astra for planning and review with local Qwen3.8-27B for implementation reportedly cut an API bill from $7.40 to $1.62 on one run; Reddit readers discussed whether Neon becomes the everyday replacement for Gemini 3.1 Pro now that Google has separate tiers for fast work versus harder projects.
items.title: Gemini 4 Neon launches as GDM's Opus/Sol contender

items.summary:
In a Guardian column, George Monbiot argues that the UK government is pursuing economic growth through datacentres and artificial intelligence in ways he believes are likely to damage rather than help the economy. He frames this as a recurring pattern in which heavily promoted sectors tend to cause economic harm, pointing to deregulation of finance before 2008 and fossil fuel subsidies as prior examples. Monbiot contends that the drive to build datacentres reflects less genuine commercial demand than the need to sustain big technology companies' share prices, citing US midterm elections where citizens voted for moratoria on new sites, after which tech stocks fell sharply. He asserts that confidence in this bubble is what keeps construction going and warns that building more enlarges it rather than resolves underlying uncertainty about whether these facilities are even needed.

Monbiot criticizes the government's classification of datacentres as nationally significant infrastructure, which lets them bypass local planning control and go directly to ministers. He claims the ostensible purpose is growth but argues their real function is sustaining tech share values that could trigger collapse. He notes the government has admitted it does not know what these facilities will be used for, while listing some actual users he disapproves of: gambling and pornography operations, including child sexual abuse imagery whose reports reportedly rose 8,400% in two years; shitposters; fascists using algorithms to amplify content; and Russian cyber-attackers. He urges readers to accept the environmental costs—landscape destruction, blocked sunlight, light pollution, aquifer depletion, pollutants, energy consumption, and climate acceleration—and even job losses as necessary for national priority.

Monbiot warns that AI companies may be overvalued and datacentres possibly overbuilt, with only a few firms likely to succeed while others are left with expensive dead infrastructure. He argues governments should pause to observe how the sector develops rather than committing prematurely, since decommissioning costs could fall on the public if other failed industries are any guide. On policy front, he says Burnham's government is turbocharging datacentres to make the UK attractive to AI firms while continuing what he calls Keir Starmer's war against pleasant surroundings and good lives. He mentions a still-pushed regulating for growth bill that would create regulatory sandboxes where corporations can do things banned elsewhere, possibly including planned AI growth zones.

Monbiot also attacks efforts to remove the Aarhus convention costs cap—guaranteed by the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018—which could force objectors to pay life-changing or home-losing bills and shut down public participation. He cites a Spotlight on Corruption investigation finding that between July 2024 and June 2026, ministers met representatives from 137 businesses some multiple times, while meeting only two community groups and no environmental organizations. A submission by the Sovereign AI Leadership taskforce representing Nvidia, Microsoft, Cisco and similar firms reportedly warned of one year to force new datacentres through before public objections become overwhelming. He notes residents of Brick Lane discovered that even social housing—the prime minister's proclaimed defining purpose—is being displaced by these projects.

Monbiot concludes that while the government has classified climate activists and Palestine protesters as national security threats, he considers the genuine threat to lie in the highest offices of state rather than among ordinary citizens. He asserts this administration is as easily influenced by commercial interests as Starmer's was, describing an industry at odds with most people's aspirations for a decent life.

No visual element: the article contains no tables or figures worth charting; its key statistics are rhetorical claims and narrative points rather than comparable data series.
items.title: Monbiot: UK's datacentre push bets on an AI bubble

items.summary: Inox Solar Americas LLC has moved its 3 GW solar cell manufacturing plant in Greenville, North Carolina into the equipment installation phase while keeping the facility on schedule for commercial production in the second quarter of 2027. The factory spans 515,460 square feet and will supply domestic monocrystalline cells directly to company module assembly operations, producing Galaxion cell architecture alongside Gamma Series monofacial and Vega Series bifacial panels. The Greenville project builds on Inox Clean Energy's acquisition of Boviet Solar U.S. manufacturing assets, which included an established 3 GW module footprint paired with a planned cell expansion; by using existing infrastructure rather than starting from scratch, the company is avoiding greenfield timelines that have delayed domestic manufacturing efforts. This expansion addresses a structural mismatch in the U.S. solar supply chain: cumulative domestic module assembly capacity has surged past 75 GWdc to 80 GWdc, while operational cell manufacturing capacity sits lower at roughly 20 GWdc, with upstream wafer and polysilicon capacities lagging further behind at approximately 3 GWdc and 10 GWdc. Because of these gaps, domestic cell makers will continue relying on qualified non-Foreign Entity of Concern wafer imports in the near term. Bringing 3.0 GW of cell capacity online is designed to help utility-scale developers navigate federal procurement rules under updated Section 45X tax credit guidelines and trade provisions, which place pressure on project developers to prove non-restricted component origins to capture domestic-content bonus credits. To meet these requirements, the Greenville plant integrates automated inline testing, precision processing, and production-record traceability. Industry analysts note that transitioning a domestic cell fab from equipment installation to commercial output remains an operational test requiring cleanroom discipline and process engineering. Ashok Nair, President and CEO of Inox Solar Americas, said: "By bringing cell technology, module manufacturing, and quality control together within our manufacturing platform, we are strengthening our ability to support customers with supply and bankability required for project pipelines."
items.title: Inox Solar Americas advances 3 GW U.S. solar cell facility to equipment installation phase

items.summary: According to Mercom India's Q3 and Nine-Months 2026 Solar Open Access Market Report, India added a record 8.4 GW of open-access solar capacity during the first nine months of 2026, up 29% from the same period in 2025. Open-access solar lets commercial and industrial consumers procure electricity from off-site projects through the grid rather than relying solely on local distribution companies. Growth was driven by greater adoption of captive ownership models and long-term power purchase agreements, while a temporary exemption from Approved List of Models and Manufacturers List-II requirements for eligible open-access projects improved access to lower-cost solar modules and supported project economics. Capacity additions slowed in the third quarter, with 2.3 GW added versus 3.4 GW in the preceding quarter and down 8% from 2.5 GW a year earlier. Priya Sanjay, managing director of Mercom India, attributed this slowdown to rising module prices, supply constraints, grid connectivity delays, and regulatory uncertainty, while noting that open-access economics remain compelling but inconsistent policies and execution bottlenecks are limiting the market's full potential. Rajasthan led quarterly additions with 29% of installations, followed by Tamil Nadu and Gujarat; the five leading states accounted for 83% of third-quarter capacity. Cumulative installed open-access solar reached 39.3 GW by end-September 2026, with Karnataka holding a 21% share, Rajasthan at 16%, and Maharashtra at 15%.
items.title: India's record open-access solar additions in first nine months of 2026

items.summary:
The International Energy Agency's new World Energy Outlook 2026 examines how the largest oil supply shock on record could accelerate the shift toward electric vehicles and solar power. The article frames this as a key takeaway from the report, noting that the longer the Strait of Hormuz crisis persists, the stronger countries' incentives become to move cars off oil and generate more electricity domestically. Initially, the world had some protection: well-stocked inventories buffered the first shock while the IEA coordinated emergency reserve releases, Gulf crude took routes around the strait, Atlantic Basin exporters shipped additional volumes, and China sharply cut its crude imports. Now consumers bear a larger share of the burden through higher prices and reduced consumption. IEA executive director Fatih Birol said that although the energy sector and global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper its effects will be.

The report observes EV sales rising in some countries affected by the crisis, alongside increased trade in solar panels and batteries. For nations heavily dependent on imported oil and gas, switching to EVs and heat pumps can reduce exposure to future fuel price spikes. Dave Jones of Ember described Hormuz as an event whose full impact is only just becoming clear, arguing it will speed up electrification and renewables faster than many expect, with much of the momentum for electrification at COP31 driven by the desire for cheaper and more secure energy. Solar leads renewable growth in every scenario the IEA models, nuclear power grows strongly, and energy efficiency and biofuels could also gain ground. The push toward homegrown energy might play out differently across parts of Asia, where some oil- and gas-importing countries have abundant domestic coal they could burn longer.

The article notes electricity demand has grown twice as fast as overall energy demand since 2019, outpacing global economic growth, driven by industrial motors, air conditioners, EVs, heat pumps, and data centers. Electricity approaches roughly 30% of the world's actual energy use by 2035 in each exploratory scenario.

On oil bypassing Hormuz, around 20 million barrels a day previously moved through the strait before the crisis. If shipping remains risky, new pipelines could route some barrels around it while buyers seek other suppliers or reduce consumption; under those conditions the IEA projects throughput falling to 8.5 million barrels a day by 2030 and below 2 million by 2035, with the Middle East still remaining the world's largest oil-exporting region. If the conflict resolves instead, oil and gas supply could rebound, while a delayed wave of liquefied natural gas might ease prices even as buyers refill inventories, and faster electrification could remove some demand from both markets.

The report also states that for the first time the world now uses more energy to cool buildings than to heat them. By 2035 the global population is expected to grow by 650 million and the economy by a third, with gradual rises in advanced economies, slowing growth in China, and faster increases led by India and Southeast Asia among emerging and developing economies.

On AI's energy footprint, under the IEA's Stated Policies Scenario global data center electricity use doubles to 1,000 terawatt-hours by 2030. That buildout is already hitting grid and supply chain constraints and facing local opposition in some places, while the agency flags risks to critical mineral supplies and threats to energy infrastructure from natural hazards and cyberattacks.

On climate outcomes, energy-related CO2 emissions stay near current levels under present policies, begin falling under stated policies, and drop further in the Additional Response Case examining stronger government responses to the crisis. Even those deeper cuts fall short of what climate goals require; the current and stated policy scenarios point to 2.5C to 2.9C of warming, with national pledges showing little sign countries are accelerating energy-sector emissions reductions.

The article also raises an immediate cost: although more people gained access to electricity and clean cooking in 2025, higher fuel prices and shortages threaten that progress, leaving around 720 million people without electricity and nearly 2 billion still relying on polluting fuels or technologies. The piece concludes with a promotional segment for EnergySage's solar installer matching service.
items.title: IEA's World Energy Outlook 2026 links Strait of Hormuz crisis to faster EV and solar adoption

items.summary: Crude oil prices steadied after an earlier weekly decline, as concerns over a return to oversupply and ongoing attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz largely canceled each other out. At the time of writing, Brent crude traded at $92.01 per barrel and West Texas Intermediate at $83.00 per barrel. Forecasters warn of an impending glut even though tanker tracking data shows flows out of the Persian Gulf remain below pre-war levels, despite a significant improvement from the war's early months. Vortexa reported that Iran has designated more than 50% of the tankers used by Gulf petrostates to move their oil through the Strait of Hormuz and on toward the Gulf of Oman and global markets. The analytics firm noted that these restrictions have not yet reduced the volume of oil moving through a shuttle relay system, with exporters adapting by adding an extra stage of ship-to-ship transfers. This has helped maintain steady outflows from the Persian Gulf, though risks persist as Iran issues daily reports of tankers striking mines in the Strait of Hormuz while attempting to move outside the channel Tehran has designated for free movement. Ing commodity strategists warned that further disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz remain an important upside risk, but rising OPEC+ output, resilient Russian exports, and building US inventories point toward a more comfortable supply picture. Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey added they expect the oil market to gradually rebalance, which would curb prices' potential for sustained upward movement. Additional downward pressure came from the U.S. Federal Reserve, which has signaled it may raise rates in December, weighing on demand growth and further limiting any upside for crude prices.
items.title: Oil Prices Steady as Hormuz Tanker Threats Offset Supply Glut Fears

items.summary: At The New York Times DealBook Summit, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk publicly supported former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and signaled his disagreement with the board's decision to remove him from the company. During the event, Musk compared Huang favorably to Michael Jordan at his peak, describing him as a figure of great importance to any team. In a separate post on X, Musk added that Huang is 'one of the most talented entrepreneur-CEOs in history.' The remarks underscored Musk's continued admiration for Huang's leadership and entrepreneurial abilities.
items.title: Musk praises ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang

items.summary:
The article reports that Nvidia, a leading American maker of AI chips, delivered strong financial results with significant growth in both earnings and revenue. This performance is attributed to rising demand for the company's chips as technology firms worldwide purchase them to build AI data centers and improve their capabilities. Despite these solid numbers, investor sentiment remains cautious amid uncertainty surrounding leadership.

The primary source of concern is CEO Jensen Huang's recent resignation from Nvidia. The article notes that Huang played a crucial role in building the company into one of the world's leading AI chip makers. Compounding the uncertainty, signals suggesting his non-return have further heightened anxiety among investors about whether new leadership can maintain the company's rapid growth and dominant market position.

The piece frames Nvidia as more than just a chip maker but rather one of the most important companies in the AI industry, with its technology used across data centers, AI models, and advanced computing. Investors are now watching how leadership changes might affect confidence throughout the broader AI chip sector, though strong demand for AI chips keeps possibilities open for continued business growth.

The article concludes by noting that investors will focus on Nvidia's new leadership, future strategy, and ongoing demand for AI chips in coming days. The company's central challenge is to demonstrate that its earnings, technological advantage, and market grip remain solid despite the change in leadership.
items.title: Nvidia's Strong Earnings Offset by Jensen Huang Departure Concerns

items.summary:
Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 a share, edging past the $70 to $78 range it had guided for an original planned offering of 825 million shares. The deal totals $81 billion and would make it the largest IPO ever, surpassing SpaceX's reported $75 billion collection when it went public in June (which reached $85.7 billion after its underwriters exercised their overallotment option). Anthropic priced above that range because investors asked to buy several times as much stock as the company put up for sale. The offering totals 980,000,000 Class A common stock shares, of which Anthropic is selling 956,351,354 and certain selling stockholders are selling 23,648,646; the company receives no proceeds from that latter portion. The offering should put Anthropic's fully diluted valuation at roughly $1.5 trillion, and it is expected to close on Nov. 20, subject to customary closing conditions.

The stock is set to begin trading on Nasdaq under the symbol ANT on Thursday, with a 30-day option granted to its underwriters to buy up to 147,000,000 more Class A common shares. Amazon and Google are expected to own about 28% of Anthropic in aggregate after the IPO and a concurrent private placement of about $26 billion; Microsoft and Google are among seven companies that agreed to buy non-voting Class N stock in that placement at the IPO price, though the purchase depends on the IPO being completed.

New York City Comptroller Mark Levine has criticized Anthropic's governance plans for the offering and urged the company in an Oct. 14 letter to pause the IPO. Anthropic's filing lists a single share of Class F stock held by a founders' entity that carries 50.1% of total voting power, meaning the company will be a controlled company under Nasdaq rules with its seven co-founders and an independent trust remaining in charge after the listing.
items.title: Anthropic prices IPO at $83 per share in record offering

items.summary: Funeral directors report an increase in direct cremations, where no mourners attend, following the Covid-19 pandemic. Brian Ugalde, whose firm has operated in Cornwall for 135 years, said non-attendance became more acceptable after lockdowns when families were not always permitted to be present. He described a funeral as "a ceremony...a farewell, a celebration" meant for those left behind, but noted direct cremation grew practical and cheaper once the model gained acceptance. SunLife's 2026 Cost of Dying Report found that around one in five funerals in the UK now involve direct cremation, with most cases arranged or requested by the deceased before death. In 86% of those instances, families held a separate celebration of life later. Andrew Judd from The Association of Funeral Directors warned that families often do not realise what is included when purchasing such plans; he stated the average cost of a direct cremation is £1,628, covering collection of the deceased, cremation somewhere in the country, and return of ashes to the family. He contrasted this with an attended funeral service, which can range from £4,200. John Ware of Walter C Parsons funeral directors in Plympton suggested families discuss unattended plans beforehand so relatives understand what to expect, noting options exist between a direct cremation and a full traditional funeral that balance lower cost with attendable services. Plymouth's The Park crematorium, which opened in 2024, has recently reduced the price of direct cremation, citing cheaper rates from other crematoria and national companies. Graham Smith at Plymouth City Council questioned why residents should use national providers when local facilities are available. Rising VAT, coffin wood costs, and fuel prices have increased traditional funeral expenses, though views in Plymouth remain mixed: Andrew Statton said a later memorial service makes no difference to him; Ann Roberts would consider direct cremation for savings and flexibility but stressed the importance of discussing wishes with family; Pam Brinkhurst preferred traditional funerals where families are present; and Phoenix Elson chose to pay more so her son could attend. Simplicity, a national provider, said its nationwide network keeps fees competitive while offering local options as a positive development.
items.title: Rise of direct cremation since pandemic

items.summary:
The Scottish government is facing scrutiny over plans to issue its first-ever bonds, nicknamed "kilts" after UK gilts. The scheme aims to raise about £1.5bn by the end of the parliamentary term, with proceeds earmarked for long-term capital projects such as building hospitals and maintaining roads. Former First Minister Humza Yousaf commissioned initial work in 2023 following recommendations from an investor panel that bonds could boost Scotland's profile and attract investment. In November last year, the government announced it had received a credit rating identical to the UK's score, based on "prudent fiscal management" and economic stability, though ministers were warned this could change if Scotland moved toward independence. David McMillan of the University of Stirling told Holyrood's finance committee that there is no perfect time to launch bonds, given ongoing market volatility from conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East.

The government expects the bonds to be issued within the current financial year, subject to market conditions. It wants to raise £1.5bn by 2031, which would represent only a fraction of its near £70bn budget. About four-fifths of the Scottish government's budget goes toward resource spending on day-to-day costs such as NHS funding, benefits payments and salaries, while capital spending covers long-term physical assets like buildings, bridges and road maintenance. The government cannot borrow for resource spending other than to correct forecasting errors, but can borrow up to £450m a year at 2023-24 levels toward a total cap of £3bn for capital spending, which is subject to inflationary uprating; adjusted for inflation this equates to about £491m in the current financial year against a limit of about £3.3bn.

Economists have noted that Scottish bonds would be more costly than existing borrowing routes through the UK government's National Loans Fund. It has been estimated externally that interest rates on "kilts" would run 0.3 percentage points above gilts, plus an additional £2m per bond in administrative costs. The Scottish government has not released costings, citing market sensitivities, but insists issuing bonds represents value for money relative to the UK scheme and argues it offers a chance to market the country while providing useful flexibility if Scotland becomes independent. Dr Ben Cormier of University of Strathclyde told Holyrood's finance committee that although Scottish bonds might cost marginally more than the UK scheme, they would "bring flexibility to public finances and debt management." McMillan agreed with the plans in principle but warned investors could lose credibility if maturities were limited to five years. Cormier cautioned that independence was the one factor that could materially change the nature of risk associated with Scottish bonds. Conservative MSP Liam Kerr raised concerns about higher costs than borrowing through the National Loans Fund and a lack of transparency, prompting McMillan to stress the need for "full information" and "a clear, full and frank conversation with the public."
items.title: Scotland's plan for its first government bonds

items.summary:
The Bank of England is undertaking a secretive, major renovation of its Grade I-listed headquarters on Threadneedle Street in the City of London. Governor Andrew Bailey oversees what his team describes as an "incredibly complex project" aimed at modernising the historic building while 3,500 staff remain working on site. The scheme seeks to preserve Roman mosaic floors, stone columns and vaulted ceilings while transforming parts of the neoclassical structure into a Google-like workplace with friendly office spaces, breakout rooms and in-house cafes.

The Bank plans for 1,400 staff currently based at its nearby office on 20 Moorgate to relocate to Threadneedle Street by summer 2028, while others take voluntary redundancy or move to a new outpost being refurbished in Leeds. Funding will come from an estimated £100m of annual savings over three years generated through 450 redundancies and other cost cuts.

Bailey's team is keen to avoid the delays and budget overruns that plagued the US Federal Reserve revamp, which grew from an initial $921m (£696m) in February 2020 to a projected final cost of nearly $2.5bn with completion pushed to December 2027. The Bank's project is smaller by comparison and pales against the possible £60bn Palace of Westminster renovation, though it resembles the £80m Elizabeth Tower restoration that Bailey wants to avoid becoming another subject of parliamentary scrutiny.

The scheme was first announced in July 2025 with work due to start this month. The construction contract went only to Sir Robert McAlpine in October, a month later than planned. A Bank spokesperson said all procurement processes aim to deliver value for money and that there will be no delays following the appointment of architects last November.

Bailey's team is based in the Parlours and must weigh cost implications from new fire safety regulations, accessibility requirements, electrical testing, plumbing upgrades and renewable heating needs. Security concerns are significant: Bailey wants to ensure 400,000 bars of gold worth more than £200bn and £100m of bank notes in the vaults remain safe from terrorists and thieves during construction.

The fate of the Bank's museum presents a further complication. The public-facing museum on Bartholomew Lane currently receives about 100,000 visitors a year, mainly schoolchildren. Some senior staff wanted to relocate it into the central quad so visitors could enter through the main entrance, while others favoured cafe space near the entrance to make the Bank appear more modern.

Vivienne Grafton, executive director of central operations, told the Architects Journal that this is an opportunity "to breathe new life into a legacy building, not through radical reinvention, but through thoughtful, intelligent transformation." However, architectural plans have yet to be agreed with the City of London Corporation and Historic England. Anna Joynt, a senior architect at Allies and Morrison, noted it was common for preparatory works to begin before full listed building consent is granted.

There has been some tangible progress: the roof of the main portico is clad in scaffolding for repairs, and last year planning permission secured an overhaul of one small section known as the former governor's secretaries' offices. The rest of the 1.4-hectare (3.5-acre) site remains uncertain.

The Bank began in rented premises in 1694 before moving to Threadneedle Street in 1734, earning its nickname "the Old Lady of Threadneedle Street" from a satirical cartoon of William Pitt the Younger. It was refashioned by Sir John Soane between 1788 and 1833 and remodelled again in the 1920s when much of the interior was demolished and rebuilt.

The building is owned by the Bank, which Gordon Brown gave independence to set interest rates in 1997. After the 2008 financial crash, it later received responsibility for regulating the banking sector under George Osborne.
items.title: Bank of England's £160m headquarters revamp faces cost fears

items.summary: South Korea's exports surpassed US$1 trillion for 2025 on Thursday (Nov 19), making it the fourth country globally to reach the milestone after Germany, the United States and China. The trade ministry reported that this figure compares with last year's record of US$709 billion. According to the trade ministry, exports passed the mark amid a global boom in AI investment driving both export volumes and related investments. South Korea is home to leading chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. President Lee Jae Myung posted on X that now the achievement must be turned into sustainable growth by enhancing competitiveness of major industries and growing future engines such as AI and bio, adding that exports should improve people's lives through 'growth for all,' sharing opportunities with both large and small companies across regional areas. The Lee administration plans to create a 162.3 trillion won (US$121.94 billion) Future Response Fund to channel excess tax revenue from the chip boom toward growth industries, young people, regional development and education. Finance minister projections indicate economic growth quickening to the mid-3 per cent range this year on record chip exports, after expanding 1 per cent last year. However, domestic demand remains weak as export benefits have not yet reached many households; consumer sentiment has been weighed down by high interest rates and prices alongside unprecedented volatility in the domestic stock market.
items.title: South Korea Becomes Fourth Country to Reach US$1 Trillion in Exports

items.summary: Grand Theft Auto VI launched globally on Thursday (Nov 19), and Sensor Tower estimates that three-quarters of the roughly 17 million units sold are on PlayStation, outselling Xbox maker Microsoft. Analysts expect this to provide a major boost to Sony's PlayStation business worldwide, though not in its home market of Japan, where GTA is considered niche. In Tokyo, shares rose about 2.8 per cent versus flat trading for the benchmark index. Toyo Securities analyst Hideki Yasuda said current Japanese trends do not suit such games and that there is no need for them to sell well there; Nintendo's Switch 2 dominance and consumer preference for anime-style titles over realistic Western games are cited as factors. Consumer Sorataka Goto, shopping in Akihabara, noted the game was only on PS5 and Xbox with multiplayer online unavailable yet, saying she would consider buying it once PC support arrives. Elsewhere, Sony's movie Spider-Man: Brand New Day succeeded globally but faced competition from Chiikawa the Movie: The Secret of Mermaid Island in Japan. Analysts expect GTA VI to soften the decline in PS5 hardware sales and support software growth; Sony sold 2.6 million PS5 units during the July to September quarter, down from 4 million a year earlier, which analysts attribute partly to demand ahead of the launch. Bernstein analyst David Dai wrote that he has modeled PlayStation profits materially ahead of Street expectations over the next couple of quarters on account of GTA VI. The release also bolsters Sony's slate after it delayed God of War Laufey by three months to May 2027. Separately, analysts expect procurement challenges as memory chip costs have risen sharply due to the AI boom; Yasuda said he does not sense Sony has much desire to aggressively sell hardware and that royalties will benefit the company enormously.
items.title: GTA VI Launch Boosts Sony Globally, Not in Japan

items.summary: The International Energy Agency warned on Thursday (Nov 19) that the Middle East conflict, which began in February following US and Israeli strikes on Iran, has created "the largest threat" to energy security in history. In its flagship annual World Energy Outlook report, the agency stated that consumers are increasingly bearing the cost as the world exhausts its ability to absorb the impact of the crisis on energy supplies. The disruption stems from Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on tankers in the region; despite US efforts to escort vessels through the channel, which previously carried about one-fifth of global oil shipments, supply lines remain severely disrupted. IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol wrote in his foreword that "the Strait of Hormuz crisis has created the largest threat to energy security in history, one that dwarfs the scale of the oil shocks of the 1970s." He noted that producing nations have brought more supplies into the market and used alternative routes, while China bought less from international markets. Birol added that "governments have intervened to try and provide some shelter for consumers, but they have nonetheless faced higher prices and, in some cases, shortfalls of supply," with increasingly falling to consumers and high prices to absorb the impact as other buffers are depleted. The agency cautioned that this crisis would leave lasting marks like previous energy shocks. Birol had struck a more hopeful tone in July when he wrote that the oil market was still benefiting from "several cushioning factors." For this report, the IEA added two additional scenarios based on what might occur if the Middle East crisis persists; while the agency acknowledged considerable resilience in the energy sector and global economy, Birol stated that "the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be" and expressed no credible pathway for the energy world to return to its prior state. The report arrives as nations convene for COP31 climate talks in Turkey amid pressure following a year of European heatwaves and wildfires plus deadly floods in Nepal. The IEA uses three scenarios: one reflecting current policies, a middle scenario incorporating stated government policies including unadopted measures, and a third envisioning net zero emissions by 2050; under the middle scenario, global oil demand is forecast to peak around 2030 before slow decline while gas demand would rise until roughly 2035.
items.title: IEA warns Mideast crisis is largest threat to energy security in history

items.summary:
Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 a share on Wednesday, ahead of Thursday's debut under the ticker ANT on Nasdaq. The price sits well above the $70 to $78 range set in filings with US regulators, and the company increased the size of the offering. At that valuation, the 825 million shares originally offered alone would raise more than $68bn. A private placement at the same price with investors including Nvidia, Google and AMD adds at least $26bn more, pushing the total past the $86.2bn SpaceX raised in June. Counting all its shares, Anthropic would be worth about $1.5tn.

The company's revenue growth has been steep: it booked $376 million in Q1 2025 and $16.96bn in the third quarter of 2026, an increase of 1,127% year on year. Anthropic's annualised revenue reached $81bn at the end of October, up about $10bn from a month earlier. More than 11,900 customers now spend over $100,000 a year, and computing costs fell to 58% of revenue in that quarter from one and a half times revenue a year prior. Its $104bn net loss for the first nine months comes almost entirely from accounting revaluations expected to disappear with the listing; excluding stock-based pay and donations, operations made a $2.5bn profit in Q3.

Analysts view the debut as a test of the wider AI trade. David Morrison of Trade Nation noted the offering was over six times subscribed. Thahbib Rahman of Block Scholes pointed out that Bitcoin fell 19% in the 50 days before SpaceX began trading and is down 23% over the same stretch ahead of Anthropic, though he suggested this latest sell-off ties more closely to a broader rout in risk assets than to investors rotating out of crypto. Jay Peters of NewEdge Wealth considered the $1.2-1.4T valuation reasonable given the business trajectory, while Richard Reyle of Questar Capital Partners called Nvidia "the Jenga tower of the whole AI trade".

Meanwhile, Nvidia is heading for a seventh straight weekly loss, its longest since July 2008. Shares fell 2.9% on Wednesday to $150.96 after quarterly results that beat expectations but failed to calm investors; the stock has lost about 35% of its value since October's start. Jensen Huang resigned on 12 November following reports about his private life and an internal investigation, with Colette Kress now serving as interim CEO.

On Monday, the US Commerce Department introduced licence requirements for advanced chips shipped to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil, which it considers at higher risk of diversion. It also requires licences for data centres anywhere that rent large amounts of computing power to Chinese companies. Peters sees the market moving toward "a slower-for-longer buildout" as borrowing costs rise and politics tightens.

Notably, Nvidia itself is among those lining up in the IPO, ready to invest more than $10bn into Anthropic, whose chief executive its founder spent years arguing with. Whether Thursday becomes a turning point or high-water mark will depend less on first-day trading than on what Anthropic reports in subsequent quarters.
items.title: Anthropic's record IPO proceeds as Nvidia faces its worst losing streak since 2008

items.summary: According to its most recent tax filing, the Musk Foundation distributed nearly $400 million in giving during 2025. The majority of that total went to another organization controlled by Musk: more than $310 million was directed to "The Foundation," a nonprofit he established in 2023 with plans to build a STEM-focused school and eventually a university. An additional $20 million flowed to a donor-advised fund at Fidelity Charitable, which the filing indicates Musk also controls. The reporting notes that more than three-quarters of the foundation's total giving went to these affiliated entities.
items.title: Musk Foundation's 2025 Giving Concentrated in His Own Nonprofits

items.summary: Electronics manufactured in Shenzhen, China are finding a growing market in Kenya, driven primarily by affordability and product variety. Retailers in Nairobi report that Chinese-made electronics have become increasingly popular among consumers seeking low-cost household appliances. Moses Tycoon, a Nairobi-based retailer, says products from China move faster than goods from Turkey and Italy because they offer the most affordable options available to buyers. He cited household blenders as an example, noting prices of about 1,500 Kenyan shillings (approximately $11.53) depending on the model. Tycoon also observed that the wide availability of different brands and models lets consumers select products matching their budgets and needs. According to him, affordable Chinese electronics have shifted consumer purchasing patterns in Kenya: previously only wealthy buyers could afford such goods, but China has made them accessible to everyone. The article frames Shenzhen as a major center for China's technology and manufacturing industries, with industrial clusters spanning smart devices, communications equipment, semiconductors, and intelligent manufacturing. This ecosystem is presented as supporting the city's connection to international markets. The piece notes that Shenzhen hosted the APEC CEO Summit from November 17 to 18, 2026, bringing together more than 2,000 political and business representatives from 21 APEC economies and 13 non-APEC economies, with discussions focused on regional connectivity, artificial intelligence, digital economic cooperation, and sustainable development. The article concludes by suggesting that the growing availability of Chinese electronics illustrates how international manufacturing and trade links influence everyday spending in Kenya, while noting Shenzhen's role remains part of a wider conversation about technology, affordability, and access to consumer goods.
items.title: Shenzhen Electronics Gain Market Share in Kenya

items.summary:
Chinese President Xi Jinping delivered a keynote address at the opening ceremony of the APEC CEO Summit 2026 in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, on November 18, 2026. The summit coincided with China's designation as the host for the year and marked the start of its 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) and the 25th anniversary of China's accession to the World Trade Organization. Xi framed a set of "hard questions of our times" about whether economies should open or close, cooperate or compete, adapt or cling to old approaches, and urged joint efforts to uphold peace, build bridges through opening up and cooperation, boost innovation for growth, and expand mutual benefits. He called for deeper science, technology and innovation partnerships, expanded digital economy and artificial intelligence cooperation, and a green low-carbon transition, arguing these would convert innovation strengths into drivers of Asia-Pacific economic growth.

The article illustrates the region's integration through Martin Chu, co-founder of a green technology startup whose company operates across Shenzhen, Hong Kong and Guangzhou in the Greater Bay Area. The cluster retained its position as the world's top innovation hub for a second consecutive year according to the World Intellectual Property Organization's 2026 rankings, which placed all seven of the world's leading innovation clusters within APEC economies spanning East Asia and the United States. Xi announced China's support for establishing a World Association for Bay Areas Economic Cooperation to deepen exchanges among bay areas worldwide.

The piece situates these developments against broader regional figures: 21 APEC member economies, home to about 40% of the world's population, account for nearly 50% of international trade and more than 60% of global GDP. The International Monetary Fund identified three forces shaping the region's economy in its recent outlook: an energy shock from Middle East conflict, an artificial intelligence-driven technology boom, and continued trade realignment following trade policy shocks.

Xi cited China's ninth China International Import Expo as evidence of a large open market now ranking second worldwide. One-year deals at that expo reached a record $85.45 billion, up 2.3% from the previous edition. He pointed to growth areas including new energy vehicles, smart homes, the silver economy and ice and snow tourism as sources of opportunity for businesses globally.

On economic performance, China's GDP grew 4.6% year on year in the first three quarters while trade with other APEC economies rose 23.9% to 24.07 trillion yuan ($3.6 trillion). The World Bank noted in July that China is pursuing a new phase of high-quality, productivity-led growth.

Xi emphasized China's commitment over its past 25 years as a WTO member and stated it would not waver in seeking win-win cooperation despite standing up to unilateralism and protectionism while remaining committed to multilateralism. The article presents these claims without independent verification or counter-claims beyond the source text.
items.title: Xi Jinping's APEC CEO Summit speech on Asia-Pacific economic opportunities

items.summary: Parts of Bangladesh were shut down on Thursday as supporters of exiled former prime minister Sheikh Hasina staged a week-long programme of protests, rallies, clashes, bomb blasts, and arson attacks that culminated in a nationwide lockdown. The unrest follows the government's rejection of Hasina's request for a new passport and identity card to facilitate her return in December; she has lived in exile in neighbouring India since fleeing Dhaka after violent protests forced her resignation in August 2024. To deter violence, police deployed 97 platoons of the Bangladesh Border Guard across seven districts, including Gopalganj and Faridpur, which are considered to have many Hasina supporters. The violence has spread widely: over the last 10 days, police reported dozens of crude bomb blasts and vehicles set afire in at least 28 districts, injuring several police officials and members of the public. On Wednesday night, former interim leader Muhammad Yunus's ancestral home in Chattogram was set on fire late; police said flammable substances were likely thrown into an unused ground-floor room while his paternal family living on upper floors remained safe. Hasina and Yunus's government have faced hostility from her supporters since assuming power after her ouster. In other incidents, a BNP activist was allegedly killed during a protest near Gopalganj late Tuesday; the same night saw a bomb explode outside Dhaka residence of cultural affairs minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury, while the house of a BNP lawmaker and shops belonging to BNP supporters in Gopalganj were set on fire. A bus company helper was burnt to death in Pirojpur after two buses were set alight Wednesday morning. On Thursday, authorities detained former education minister Nurul Islam Nahid from his Dhaka home; he faces charges over several killings during the 2024 protests. At least 37 branches and offices of Grameen Bank have been targeted in arson attacks or attempted fires since 10 November, with 14 more attacked since midnight Tuesday. Home minister Salahuddin Ahmed accused Awami League leaders abroad of inciting supporters to destabilise Bangladesh and torch property, adding that those involved would be identified and prosecuted; most Awami League leaders remain in hiding and could not be reached for comment. Hasina was sentenced to death by a local court on the occasion marking one year since her ouster, having been found guilty of ordering a deadly crackdown on a student-led uprising in 2024.
items.title: Violent protests and killings in Bangladesh ahead of Sheikh Hasina's planned return

items.summary: A Japanese court in Utsunomiya, Tochigi Prefecture, on Thursday sentenced an 18-year-old high school boy to 18 months in prison suspended for four years. Presiding Judge Yumiko Takashima of the Utsunomiya District Court found him guilty under the employment security law for introducing hazardous work, and public prosecutors had sought the same 18-month sentence he received. According to the indictment, on May 13 the boy introduced a 16-year-old from Kawasaki in Kanagawa Prefecture to another 16-year-old from Sagamihara, knowing that the latter would serve as the perpetrator. The robbery-murder took place at the home of Eiko Tomiyama, 69, in Kaminokawa on May 14, when she was assaulted and died later that day. Four boys aged 16 to 17 are suspected of carrying out the robbery, while two others have been indicted as alleged on-site supervisors: Kaito Takemae, 29, and his wife Miyu, 25. Kazuhiko Masuda, 48, is identified as the alleged mastermind and remains wanted internationally on suspicion of robbery and murder.
items.title: Japanese high school student sentenced for introducing robbery-murder perpetrator

items.summary: Formula One drivers welcomed a signal from FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem that the sport is moving toward new power unit regulations, with some drivers expressing hope for a return to naturally aspirated V8 engines possibly as soon as 2030. Ben Sulayem indicated on social media this week that a shift away from current V6 hybrid turbo units was imminent, writing 'You spoke, we listened. V8s coming soon…'. Formula One last used such engines between 2006 and 2013, and drivers noted the change could make cars lighter, simpler, and cheaper for manufacturers while restoring an engine roar many fans have missed in the current era. McLaren's Oscar Piastri responded to questions with 'Very,' before adding that he did not know whether the engines would match those from his youth but was glad the feedback had been heard, hoping the move would be more straightforward for fans and cheaper and simpler for manufacturers as a win-win scenario. Mercedes driver George Russell said the sound of the previous V8 era gave him goosebumps, describing it as 'the high-pitched squeal that I'm missing from this era,' while arguing Formula One should retain an electrical element to keep cars at the performance frontier; he cited wanting extra 400, 500, or 600 kilowatts of power alongside internal combustion to reach over 1,000 horsepower. Russell also cautioned that nostalgia for the final V8 years overlooked the fact that those cars were slower than today's machinery. Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli said returning to an older style would be cool and noted lighter cars as a key appeal, while two-time world champion Fernando Alonso stated he did not expect to still be racing by then, calling it frustrating that the change had not happened in 2014 after what he described as 16 or 17 lost years of pure racing.
items.title: F1 drivers welcome possible V8 engine return

items.summary: World Anteater Day falls on Nov. 19, marking recognition of tube-nosed, ant- and termite-eating animals across Central and South America that are closely related to sloths. The giant anteater (Myrmecophaga tridactyla) is the largest species and lives on the ground where it rips open anthills and termite nests with its razor-sharp claws and slurps up insects with its long, sticky tongue; the species is listed as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. Habitat destruction and hunting have pushed giant anteaters out of parts of their range, but restoration and rewilding efforts are helping them return in some former areas. In 2025, a giant anteater returned to Argentina's Alma Guaraní reserve in the Gran Chaco for the first known time since 1986, reported Mongabay contributor Sean Mowbray. Habitat degradation from agricultural expansion and forest loss had cut ant abundance by 30-50% compared with well-preserved areas, directly affecting the anteater. The Alma Guaraní Natural Reserve covers approximately 6,400 hectares (about 15,800 acres) and has hosted volunteer-led restoration for more than a decade; volunteers planted native trees in some spots while using fences to let other land regenerate naturally by excluding livestock, dogs, hunting, and fishing. A network of 20 camera traps found the anteater mostly stayed in passively restored areas, though experts caution it is too early to tell whether this return signals recovery or a one-off event and stress the need for continuous monitoring. Separately, in August 2023, Fábio Mazim's team captured footage of a giant anteater with its long snout and bushy tail at Brazil's Espinilho State Park; Mazim told contributor Sarah Brown that he shouted and cried upon seeing it and took days to grasp the importance of this record. Giant anteaters had not been seen alive in that region since 1890, and between August 2023 and February 2024 when Brown's story was published there were another 11 sightings; scientists say it is unclear whether these were the same individual but conclude it likely crossed over from Iberá Park in northeastern Argentina, where a rewilding project has released around 110 giant anteaters.
items.title: Giant anteater returns to restored habitats in Argentina and Brazil

items.summary:
China's Xi Jinping is set to host a historic summit in Shenzhen bringing together Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump, and himself for what he views as an unprecedented diplomatic achievement. The article frames this gathering as evidence that China has moved from reacting to Western decisions made in Washington, London, and Brussels toward shaping the international order itself, with the futuristic setting of driverless cars, drones, and robots underscoring Beijing's economic prominence. Although ostensibly an Asia Pacific economic summit, Xi sees it as a demonstration of China's grip on global economy and politics.

The article identifies several pitfalls for Xi despite his ambitions. On Ukraine, now in its fifth year, China is reluctant to place the war on the agenda because doing so risks damaging European connections at a time when Beijing relies heavily on exports, while also wanting to avoid destabilizing Russia, a key ally. Beijing maintains neutrality by calling for negotiations and political settlement without condemning Moscow's full-scale invasion, even as the US under Biden and Europe accuse China of supplying components and buying Russian oil and gas.

On nuclear weapons, Trump has signaled he wants the three leaders to discuss limiting global stockpiles after New START expired in February. The last major treaty had capped US and Russian warheads; its lapse triggers fears of an arms race. Beijing resists inclusion, arguing its arsenal is considerably smaller than Washington's and Moscow's, so it would be unfair for China to accept their limits while retaining freedom to develop its own capabilities.

On optics, Xi wants tight control over the meeting through choreographed speeches and talking points, but faces two unpredictable leaders who have threatened to go off script. There is a risk they dominate proceedings and reduce Xi to host rather than architect, though unscripted moments could instead highlight his preferred image as a stable senior statesman amid Putin's and Trump's ongoing wars.

Finally, the summit offers little likely outcome but projects power ahead of next year's Communist Party Congress, where Xi is expected to secure a historic fourth term. The article notes China faces domestic challenges including a property crisis denting consumer confidence, heavily indebted local governments, slowed manufacturing, rising reliance on flexible jobs without pensions or social security, and one in five young people struggling to find work. A photo-op with Putin and Trump may provide Xi propaganda that his country's century of humiliation is over and that China now shapes the rules of a new era rather than merely being a rising power.
items.title: Xi's Shenzhen Summit With Putin and Trump: Triumphs and Pitfalls

items.summary: A Brisbane Supreme Court trial will be held into the death of 12-year-old Tiffani Scholten, who police allege was murdered by her mother Carrissa Kaye Scholten and long-term partner Aaron Paul Richardson. The pair faced Southport Magistrates Court on Thursday charged with one count each of murder as a domestic violence offence after being committed to trial by Magistrate Louisa Pink following a protracted homicide investigation that began in August 2024, when the girl was found unresponsive at their home on Bellagio Crescent in Coomera, Gold Coast.
